HSTU already has a strong sampled-softmax precedent: Meta’s [official configuration](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-final.gin) uses 128 negatives, L2-normalized embeddings and temperature 0.05. These are starting points, not established Amazon optima. [Wu et al., 2024](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) show that sampled softmax emphasizes hard negatives through its gradients; temperature controls this emphasis, with excessively low temperatures allowing a few difficult negatives to dominate. Thus, larger negative pools and temperature tuning are useful controlled experiments before adding explicit mining.

Harder negatives can improve discrimination but also amplify false negatives: an unobserved, highly scored item may actually interest the user. [R²NS, WWW 2026](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports early-training failures from aggressive mining and supports uniform-negative warm-up followed by progressively harder sampling. It discusses stochastic selection among top-ranked candidates to reduce deterministic hardest-item selection. A [2024 sequential-recommendation comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds sampler-dependent popularity trade-offs; popularity-based sampling does not universally improve aggregate accuracy.

Practical hypothesis for this task: retain one HSTU per category; compare multi-negative softmax with 64–256 negatives and temperatures 0.05–0.2, then test a warm-up followed by mixed uniform and stochastic hard negatives scored by that same model. Exclude padding, the target and known training-history positives; never consult held-out labels when sampling. These ranges are proposed experiments, not published Electronics-specific findings. Select using fixed four-category macro validation HR@10, inspecting Electronics separately. Larger training margins against easy negatives alone do not establish better ranking.
